subject: Logical Reasoning
introduction: Syllogisms test your ability to draw valid conclusions from two or more given statements (premises). In SIMAK, each statement is treated as absolutely true — even if it contradicts common sense. Your task is NOT to judge truth, but to determine what MUST logically follow. Use Venn diagrams or immediate inference rules to check validity.

key_formulas.name: Universal Affirmative (A)
key_formulas.formula: \text{All A are B} \Rightarrow \text{Venn: A circle inside B circle}

key_formulas.name: Universal Negative (E)
key_formulas.formula: \text{No A are B} \Rightarrow \text{Venn: A and B circles don't overlap}

key_formulas.name: Particular Affirmative (I)
key_formulas.formula: \text{Some A are B} \Rightarrow \text{Venn: A and B overlap partially}

key_formulas.name: Particular Negative (O)
key_formulas.formula: \text{Some A are not B} \Rightarrow \text{Venn: part of A is outside B}

tips_and_tricks: Treat every statement as 100% true — even absurd ones.
Draw Venn diagrams for complex sets of premises.
'All A are B' does NOT mean 'All B are A'. The conversion is NOT always valid!
'Some A are B' is always a valid conclusion if 'All A are B' — some is included in all.
If the conclusion uses 'must be true', verify it holds in ALL possible diagrams.
Negative conclusion requires at least one negative premise.
'Either...or...' in conclusion can be true if both individual parts might be true.

worked_examples.title: Example 1: All-All syllogism
worked_examples.question: All cats are mammals. All mammals are warm-blooded. What can we conclude?
solution: Step 1: Draw chain: Cats ⊂ Mammals ⊂ Warm-blooded.
Step 2: Valid conclusion: All cats are warm-blooded (AAA-1 form).
Step 3: Also valid: Some warm-blooded are cats (by conversion of A to I).
Step 4: NOT valid: All warm-blooded are cats (illegal conversion).

worked_examples.title: Example 2: 'Some' premise complications
worked_examples.question: All A are B. Some C are A. What follows?
solution: Step 1: All A ⊂ B. Some C overlap with A.
Step 2: The C that overlap with A are also in B (since A ⊂ B).
Step 3: So some C are B.
Step 4: Valid conclusion: Some C are B. (Some C are A + All A are B → Some C are B.)

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements: All dogs are animals. All animals need food.
Conclusion: All dogs need food.
Is the conclusion valid?
questions.explanation:
**AAA-1 Syllogism:**
All dogs → animals (A ⊂ B)
All animals → need food (B ⊂ C)
Therefore All dogs → need food (A ⊂ C) ✓

This is a valid chain inference.
hints: Dogs ⊂ Animals ⊂ Need food — draw the Venn chain.
If every A is B, and every B is C, then every A is C.
Valid conclusion.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements: No fish are birds. All eagles are birds.
Conclusion: No eagles are fish.
Is the conclusion valid?
questions.explanation:
No fish are birds → Fish and Birds are completely separate.
All eagles are birds → Eagles ⊂ Birds.
Since Eagles ⊂ Birds, and Birds ∩ Fish = ∅, then Eagles ∩ Fish = ∅
Conclusion: No eagles are fish ✓
hints: Eagles are inside the Bird circle. Fish and Birds don't overlap.
Eagles (inside Birds) can't be in Fish.
No eagles are fish — valid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statement: All roses are flowers.
Conclusion I: Some flowers are roses.
Conclusion II: All flowers are roses.
Which is valid?
questions.explanation:
All roses are flowers → Roses ⊂ Flowers.

Conclusion I: Some flowers are roses → YES ✓ (if all A are B, then some B are A — called 'conversion by limitation').

Conclusion II: All flowers are roses → NOT VALID ✗ (there may be other flowers that aren't roses).
hints: Draw: Roses circle inside Flowers circle.
'Some flowers are roses' — is any part of Flowers inside Roses? Yes.
'All flowers are roses' — can flowers be outside Roses? Yes → invalid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements: Some students are athletes. All athletes are disciplined.
Conclusion: Some students are disciplined.
Is this valid?

options.text: Only if all students are athletes

questions.explanation:
Some students = athletes. Those athletes are disciplined (All athletes → disciplined).
Therefore those students (who are athletes) are disciplined.
Conclusion: Some students are disciplined ✓
hints: Some students ARE athletes. All athletes are disciplined.
The students who are athletes → disciplined.
Some students are disciplined. Valid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements: No computers are living things. All robots are computers.
Conclusion: No robots are living things.
Valid?
questions.explanation:
Robots ⊂ Computers. Computers ∩ Living things = ∅.
Since Robots ⊂ Computers, Robots ∩ Living things = ∅.
Conclusion: No robots are living things ✓
hints: Robots are inside Computers. Computers don't overlap with Living things.
Robots (inside Computers) can't reach Living things.
Valid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statement: Some A are B. Some B are C.
Conclusion: Some A are C.
Valid?

options.text: Valid only with a third premise

questions.explanation:
**Two 'Some' premises cannot guarantee a conclusion.**
A and C might not overlap at all. The B's that overlap with A might be completely different from the B's that overlap with C.

Draw: A and B overlap, B and C overlap, but A and C might be separate.
Conclusion is NOT necessarily valid.
hints: Draw a Venn: can A and C be completely separate?
The B's shared with A and the B's shared with C might be different.
Not necessarily valid — Some+Some doesn't guarantee a conclusion.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements: All X are Y. No Z are Y.
Conclusion: No Z are X.
Valid?
questions.explanation:
X ⊂ Y, and Z ∩ Y = ∅.
Since X ⊂ Y and Z can't touch Y, Z can't touch X either.
Conclusion: No Z are X ✓
hints: X is inside Y. Z can't reach Y at all.
So Z can't reach X (which is inside Y).
Valid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statement: No managers are lazy.
Conclusion: Some non-lazy people are managers.
Valid?
questions.explanation:
No managers are lazy → All managers are non-lazy.
If managers exist, then some non-lazy people are managers.
Conclusion follows if we assume the class isn't empty ✓
hints: No managers are lazy means all managers fall into 'non-lazy'.
If any manager exists, they are non-lazy.
Some non-lazy are managers — valid (assuming the class exists).

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. All politicians are liars.
2. Some honest people are politicians.
Which conclusion MUST follow?
questions.explanation:
Some honest people = politicians (from S2).
All politicians = liars (from S1).

Those honest people who are politicians → are also liars.
Conclusion: Some honest people are liars ✓

(This may seem contradictory but we treat statements as true.)
hints: The honest people who are politicians are also liars (from S1).
Some honest + All politicians are liars → Some honest are liars.
Answer: Some honest people are liars.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. All books are knowledge.
2. Some knowledge is valuable.
3. All valuable things are expensive.

Conclusion: Some knowledge is expensive.
Valid?
questions.explanation:
Some knowledge is valuable (S2). All valuable → expensive (S3).
Therefore some knowledge is expensive ✓

(The B that is valuable → also expensive, so some knowledge is expensive.)
hints: Some knowledge is valuable, and valuable → expensive.
Chain: some knowledge → valuable → expensive.
Some knowledge is expensive. Valid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. No trees are roads.
2. Some walls are roads.

Conclusion I: Some walls are not trees.
Conclusion II: No walls are trees.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation:
Some walls = roads (S2). No trees = roads (S1) → trees and roads are separate.
Those walls that are roads → are NOT trees (since trees ∩ roads = ∅).
So those particular walls are not trees → Some walls are not trees ✓ (Conclusion I)

Conclusion II 'No walls are trees' is too strong — other walls might be trees. INVALID ✗
hints: Walls that are roads can't be trees (trees and roads don't overlap).
So some walls (the ones that are roads) are not trees → Conclusion I valid.
Conclusion II 'No walls are trees' is not guaranteed — other walls could be trees.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. All circles are shapes.
2. All shapes are beautiful.
3. Some beautiful things are colorful.

Conclusion: Some circles are colorful.
Valid?

options.text: Not necessarily — the beautiful circles may not be the colorful ones
Valid only if all shapes are colorful
Valid because all circles are beautiful

questions.explanation:
All circles → shapes → beautiful.
Some beautiful things are colorful.

The colorful beautiful things might be a different subset of beautiful, not necessarily circles.
Conclusion 'Some circles are colorful' is NOT necessarily valid.

The 'some beautiful = colorful' might not overlap with circles even though circles are beautiful.
hints: All circles are beautiful, but only SOME beautiful are colorful.
Are those 'some colorful beautiful things' necessarily circles? Not required.
Not necessarily valid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text: Given: If all A are B, and all B are C, and no C are D, what can we say about A and D?
questions.explanation:
A ⊂ B ⊂ C. C ∩ D = ∅.
Since A ⊂ C and C ∩ D = ∅ → A ∩ D = ∅.
Conclusion: **No A are D** ✓
hints: Chain: A inside B inside C. D doesn't touch C.
A is inside C. D can't reach C, so D can't reach A.
No A are D.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. All cats are pets.
2. Some pets are small.
3. All small things are cute.

Conclusion I: Some cats are cute.
Conclusion II: Some pets are cute.
Which is/are valid?
questions.explanation:
Some pets are small (S2). All small → cute (S3). So some pets are cute ✓ (Conclusion II valid)

Conclusion I: Are those small pets necessarily cats? Not guaranteed — they could be other pets.
Some cats might be small, but S2 doesn't say so.
Conclusion I is NOT necessarily valid.
hints: Some pets are small → those are cute. But are those small pets cats?
The small pets could be dogs, not cats.
Conclusion II (some pets are cute) is valid. Conclusion I (some cats are cute) is not guaranteed.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements: Some doctors are singers. All singers are creative.
Conclusion: All doctors are creative.
Valid?

options.text: No — only SOME doctors are creative

questions.explanation:
Only SOME doctors are singers. Those singers (doctor-singers) are creative.
But other doctors (non-singers) — we don't know.

Conclusion 'All doctors are creative' is too strong → **INVALID**.
Correct conclusion: Some doctors are creative ✓
hints: 'Some' doctors are singers — not all.
Only those doctor-singers are definitely creative.
'All doctors are creative' is too strong → invalid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. No birds can swim.
2. Penguins can swim.
Conclusion: Penguins are not birds.
Valid?
questions.explanation:
Remember: we treat statements as ABSOLUTELY TRUE even if wrong factually.

No birds can swim → birds ∩ swimmers = ∅.
Penguins can swim → penguins ⊂ swimmers.
If penguins were birds, birds would be in swimmers — contradiction!
Conclusion: Penguins are not birds ✓ (logically valid given the premises)
hints: Treat both statements as 100% true.
No birds swim. Penguins swim → penguins can't be birds.
Valid given these premises.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. Some scientists are writers.
2. All writers are philosophers.
3. Some philosophers are not innovative.

Conclusion I: Some scientists are philosophers.
Conclusion II: Some scientists are not innovative.
Which MUST follow?
questions.explanation:
Conclusion I: Some scientists = writers (S1). All writers = philosophers (S2). Those scientist-writers → philosophers. So some scientists are philosophers ✓

Conclusion II: Those scientist-writers → philosophers. But are they non-innovative? S3 says SOME philosophers are not innovative. The scientist-philosophers might all be innovative. Conclusion II NOT necessarily valid.

Only Conclusion I follows ✓
hints: Conclusion I: Some scientists→writers→philosophers. Valid chain.
Conclusion II: Are those philosopher-scientists among the 'not innovative' ones? Not guaranteed.
Only Conclusion I is valid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. All that glitters is not gold.
2. All gold is valuable.

Conclusion: Some glittering things are not valuable.
Valid?

options.text: Valid — some glittering things are not gold and may not be valuable
Invalid — all glittering things could still be valuable through other means
Invalid — the premises don't logically connect glitter to value

questions.explanation:
S1: Some glittering things are not gold (i.e., not all glittering = gold).
S2: All gold is valuable.

The non-gold glittering things: S2 says nothing about them — they MIGHT be valuable or not.
We CANNOT conclude some glittering things are not valuable (they could all be valuable through non-gold means).

Conclusion is NOT necessarily valid.
hints: S1 says some glittering things aren't gold. Does that mean they're not valuable?
Not being gold doesn't mean not valuable — other valuable things exist.
We can't conclude some glittering things are not valuable. Invalid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. All P are Q.
2. All Q are R.
3. Some R are not S.
4. All S are T.

Conclusion: All P are T.
Valid?

options.text: Valid if all R are S
Invalid because S3 breaks the chain

questions.explanation:
Chain: P ⊂ Q ⊂ R. All P are R.
S3: Some R are not S. The P's (which are R) might or might not be S.
S4: If P were S → P are T. But if P are not S → no guarantee P is T.

We can't conclude All P are T because some P (as members of R) might not be S, giving no path to T.
hints: P→Q→R chain gives All P are R.
But some R are not S — are the P's among the S ones or non-S ones?
Not guaranteed all P are S → not guaranteed all P are T. Not necessarily valid.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. No introverts are talkative.
2. All social media influencers are talkative.
3. Some students are introverts.

Conclusion I: No students who are introverts are influencers.
Conclusion II: Some students are not influencers.
Both valid?
questions.explanation:
I: Introvert ∩ Talkative = ∅. Influencers ⊂ Talkative. So Introvert ∩ Influencer = ∅. Students who are introverts cannot be influencers ✓

II: Some students are introverts. Introverts cannot be influencers. So those students (introverts) are not influencers. Some students are not influencers ✓

Both valid!
hints: No introverts are talkative. Influencers must be talkative → introverts ≠ influencers.
Some students are introverts → those students are not influencers.
Both conclusions follow.

questions.subject: Logical Reasoning
questions.question_text:
Statements:
1. All A are B or C (A ⊂ B∪C).
2. No B are D.
3. No C are D.

Conclusion: No A are D.
Valid?
questions.explanation:
Every A is either in B or C (or both).
No B intersects D. No C intersects D.
Therefore no member of B∪C is in D.
Since every A ⊂ B∪C, no A can be in D.
Conclusion: **No A are D** ✓
hints: Every A is in B or C. Neither B nor C touches D.
Since A is covered by B∪C, and D doesn't touch either, D can't touch A.
No A are D. Valid.
